div.head: Real-time Fieldbuses are currently a signijcant issue in both process control and manufacturing areas. They constitute the base upon which real-time fault-tolerant distributed systems can be designed for these application areas. A potential large leap towards the use of Fieldbus in such timecritical applications lies in the evaluation of its temporal behuviour In particulal; an important problem associated with the Fieldbus FIP is its inability to guarantee the timing pe~ormance of sporadic trafJic. In this paper we develop the pre-run-time schedulability analysis of FIE bounding

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The growing level of automation in production and process control systems is accompanied by an increasing development of distributed time-critical applications. A significant step forward in such systems consists of the integration of these numerous time-critical applications by means of a real-time fault-tolerant Fieldbus. One important requirement of these networks is, however, the schedulability of the information flow. The scheduling strategy must guarantee the timeliness property, which can be satisfied through the evaluation of the worst case response time [2].

In real-time Fieldbus type of applications the information flow usually consists of both periodic and sporadic data traffic. Periodic traffic is generated at regular intervals and usually has hard real-time deadlines. On the other hand, sporadic traffic has stochastic inter-arrival times, i.e. their arrival times cannot be fully predicted and they are mainly generated by events.

Hard real time data traffic must be sent and received within a bounded interval (ie the deadline), otherwise a serious fault is said to occur. A soft real-time requirement relaxes this, permitting occasional timing faults, merely re-quiring some performance level to be met.

While the hard real time periodic data traffic can be guaranteed a priori by means of a static table, it remains an open issue and a difficult problem to guarantee the worst case response time and to schedule adequately the hard real time sporadic traffic, due to their probabilistic occurrence in the system.

In this paper we derive the pre-run-time schedulability analysis of the Fieldbus FIP. The goal of this analysis is precisely to evaluate the worst case response time (WCRT) of the hard real-time sporadic traffic with fixed length. This paper is organized as follows: section 2 presents the computational model that supports the basic analysis. In section 3 we present the main features of the FIP network that concerns our analysis. In section 4 we discuss previous analysis assessing the worst case response time and we also develop a new analysis to this problem. Section 5 illustrates with a numerical example the use of equations derived. We finally conclude in section 6.

div.head: Computational model, definitions and notation
div.p: We assume two classes of sporadic traffic: exchanges of identified variables and message transfers. Each variable in the distributed system is associated with an identifier that uniquely characterizes the variable. Addressing is global. Entities participating in the exchange of a variable do not physically address each other. Rather, they refer to identifiers that they recognize in production or consumption. Variable exchanges are accomplished through broadcasting.
Exchanges of messages take place in point-to-point or in multipoint. Each message transmitted contains the address or the transmitting entity and the address of the destination entity.

div.head: scheduling in FIP
div.p: FIP (Factory Instrumentation Protocol) is a French national standard for Fieldbus designed to provide links between level zero (sensordactuators) and level one devices (PLCs, controllers, etc..) in automation systems [l]. FIP adopts the producer-distributor-user (PDU) model for variable transfers. Each variable has a single producer and one or more users. A variable is not identified through station address but by its unique identifier which is a priori known by the Producer and the Users. Variable transfers are handled in three steps:
1. A central entity, the Bus arbiter (BA), broadcasts the identifier of the next periodic variable to be broadcast.
2. Each connected entity reads the identifier and the entity that recognizes itself as the Producer of that variable responds with the variable value.
3. The entities that have recognized themselves as Users of the variable capture the value and make it available to their application process(es).

From the bus access control point of view, FIP is based on a centralized TDMA MAC protocol. The BA triggers and controls all the bus accesses enabling data transfer exchanges between communicating entities. This operation can best be described by considering the nature of the data traffic, as outlined in the next subsections.

div.head: Scheduling the periodic traffic
div.p: The BA handles all periodic transfers according to a static scanning table, which contains the list of identifiers to broadcast on the bus. At configuration time the BA is given a list of identifiers to scan along with their corresponding periods. This configuration is checked for temporal consistency and once it is validated, the BA infinitely repeats the polling of the periodic variables performing the same elementary cycles. When the producer of the last variable in an elementary cycle has transmitted its value, the BA uses the remaining available time to fulfill requests for sporadic transfers. If no such request has been made, the BA transmits padding identifiers (i.e. identifiers which have no producers) to indicate to other nodes connected to the network that the system is still in operation.

div.head: Scheduling the sporadic traffic
div.p: The FIP scheduler treats the sporadic variables (i.e. variables not included in the scanning table due to their stochastic occurrence in the system) according to a three step procedure: 0 The BA broadcasts the identifier of a periodic variable A. Each connected entity reads the identifier and the entity that recognizes itself as the Producer of variable A replies with the corresponding variable value. Additionally, the Producer sets a sporadic transfer request bit in the control field of the response frame, which causes the BA to note the identifier in a queue of pending requests for variable transfers. This request can assume two priority levels: Urgent and Normal. The BA holds two independent queues for each level of priority.

Upon completion of the transmission of periodic variables in the current elementary cycle, the BA asks the Producer of the variable A for a list of the pending sporadic requests. The producer responds by sending a list of identifiers, which is stored in another queue by the BA. A response frame can hold from 1 up to 64 identifiers. The BA may transmit the identification request frame very soon after the request is noted, or much later. The service delay depends on the periodic traffic load and the requests in progress.

The BA starts fulfilling the requests as it does with the periodic variables, i.e. by broadcasting the identifier of the variable to be exchanged and waiting for the response of the Producer. The number of requests that the BA fills initially depends on the availability of remaining time in the current elementary cycle. Unfulfilled requests are postponed to the next elementary cycle. A node can only request sporadic transfers using responses to variables that it produces and that are configured in the cyclic traffic.

The principle for a sporadic message transfer is similar. For example, the unacknowledged message transfer request has three stages to the mechanism: 0 The BA calls for identifier A. The producer of A replies with the value of A and indicates in the frame control field that it has a request for sporadic message transfer.

0 In the acyclic phase, the BA gives the producer of the identifier A the righ to transmit. The producer of A then transmits its message. This message includes its address and the address of the destination nodes. The BA then waits to receive a frame indicating that the message transfer transaction is completed.
0 After sending its message on the bus the transmitter of the message returns control of the bus to the BA.

The analysis presented can be used without further extensions to study the schedulability of hard real time sporadic messages, variables or alternatively a traffic pattern composed of a mix of variable and message sets. This is due to the fact that the mechanisms used to schedule sporadic variables and messages are similar, except that the later requires an extra overhead, including two extra short control frames for acknowledged services and one for unacknowledged services. However, this additional overhead can be taken into account in the analysis when evaluating the value of C*. In order to reduce the pessimism of the analysis, it is required in practice to make the value for the length C* of variables and messages as close as possible.

Equation ( 8) is a generic one, it can be applied to a wide range of centralized scheduling protocols in Fieldbus multiaccess networks, such as IECLSA-SPSO, with minor modifications. The demonstration of this property is, however, outside the scope of this paper.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper we have studied some properties of the FIP network that concerns the pre-schedulability analysis of its data traffic response times. Fundamentally, we have derived the worst case response time equation of hard real-time sporadic traffic for the centralized static scheduling algorithm implemented in FIP. We have also extended the analysis to cope with arbitrary deadlines. The analysis reported enables the FIP protocol to be used in a wide range of real-time applications. This analysis gives a sufficient and necessary condition to the calculation of the schedulability of all sporadic traffic.
